transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. Well, I'm here because... I guess it's my eating habits. It's really just gotten completely out of hand lately, especially at night. I work as a marketing manager, so I’m constantly running around, managing events, taking people out, and my days are just incredibly packed. But the real issue isn't during the day. It's when I get home. 

After everyone goes to bed and the house is finally quiet, I'll go down to the kitchen. I always tell myself, you know, "I'm just going to have a little bite of some leftovers." Just a taste, just to wind down. But then... I don't even know how it happens, it's like I blink and I realize I’ve eaten just a massive amount of food. Like the other night, I brought home half a tray of catered pasta from a campaign launch, and I ate the entire thing. And it didn't stop there, I also ate this incredibly rich dessert I had boxed up from a client dinner earlier in the week, and then I just started opening cabinets and eating whatever snacks were in the pantry. Pretzels, granola bars, just... whatever I could find. And this was all in one sitting. I just start with the intention of having one little bite of leftovers, and suddenly I've eaten enough for five people in a single stretch, and I just... I really need help figuring out why I'm doing this.
After these nighttime eating episodes, do you ever try to compensate for the amount of food you've eaten, like making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or exercising excessively?

No, no, I don't do any of that. I mean, the thought has crossed my mind, I won't lie, especially when I wake up the next morning feeling so unbelievably full and just... sick to my stomach, physically and emotionally. I'll lay there in bed and think, "God, I wish I could just undo all of that." But actually making myself throw up? No, I've never been able to do that. The idea of it just terrifies me, honestly. And laxatives, I've never even bought them. I remember a girl in my sorority in college who messed up her whole digestive system with those, and that always stuck with me, so I steer clear. 

As for exercise... well, I have this gym membership, right? It's one of those really nice boutique places near my office, and I pay an absolute fortune for it every month. I always tell myself I'm going to go before work, especially after a bad night of eating. I'll even set out my workout clothes—these matching sets I bought specifically to motivate myself—and I'll set my alarm for 5:30 AM. But when the alarm goes off, I'm just so exhausted from staying up late eating, and my stomach feels so heavy and awful, that I just hit snooze. I end up sleeping in until the very last second and then rushing to get to the office for my morning meetings. So, no, I don't exercise to make up for it. I barely exercise at all these days, which just adds to the guilt, you know? I just sit with it. I sit with the fullness and the shame all day at work while I'm trying to smile and pitch campaigns to clients.
Do these nighttime eating episodes usually happen after a particularly stressful or emotionally difficult day, or do they seem to occur regardless of how your day went emotionally?

Well, it's... it's definitely tied to stress, yes. I mean, my job is stressful, like I said, but honestly, the really bad nights, the ones where I eat the most, they almost always happen after things are tense at home. My husband and I, we've just been going through this rough patch lately. He works in finance, long hours too, and we just sort of pass each other in the hallway most days. But when we do interact, especially in the evenings, it can get so snippy. Just last Tuesday, we had this incredibly stupid argument about who was supposed to call the plumber to fix the guest bathroom sink. It was ridiculous, but it escalated, and he just went upstairs and shut the bedroom door. 

And that's when it happens. I'm left downstairs, feeling so angry and misunderstood and just... lonely, I guess. So I go to the kitchen. And it's like... once I take that first bite, especially after a fight like that, something just shifts. It's like the decision-making part of my brain just completely goes offline. I'll be standing there, eating cold pasta straight out of the Tupperware, and there's this voice in my head, loud and clear, saying, "Patricia, stop. This is enough. You're not even hungry anymore." I'm literally thinking those exact words. But my hand just keeps moving. I keep reaching for more food, opening another bag of chips, slicing another piece of cheese. It’s like I'm watching myself do it from the outside, but I have absolutely no power to stop my own hands. I just lose all control, completely and utterly, until I'm so full it physically hurts.
When these nighttime eating episodes happen, are you fully awake and aware of what you're doing the whole time?

Yes, yes, I'm completely awake. It's not like sleepwalking or anything like that, though sometimes I wish it were, because then maybe I'd have a better excuse, you know? But no, I am fully conscious. I know exactly where I am, I know I'm standing in my kitchen, usually in my bare feet on the cold tile, and the only light is from the refrigerator or the little pendant light over the island. I'm completely aware of what I'm doing. 

Like I was saying before, I can hear that voice in my head telling me to stop. I can feel the texture of the food, I can taste it—well, at first anyway. After a while, honestly, I stop tasting it and it just becomes this mechanical motion. But I'm awake for all of it. I remember opening the containers, I remember the crinkle of the bags, I remember the exact sequence of what I ate. Like, first the pasta, then the dessert, then the pretzels. I remember every single detail. It's just that the awareness doesn't translate into any kind of action to stop myself. It's the most frustrating thing in the world, being so hyper-aware of your own behavior but feeling like a passenger in your own body while it happens. So, yes, I'm definitely awake. I'm painfully awake for every single bite.
Can you describe what you’re feeling emotionally in the moment while you’re eating—do you feel numb, detached, or like you’re not really there?

Numb? Um... I don't, I don't really know if numb is the right word. I mean, I'm not sure exactly what you mean by detached or not being there, because like I was just saying, I feel very much there. I'm painfully present for the whole thing. If anything, it’s the exact opposite of numb. It’s like the volume on every single emotion is just cranked all the way up to ten. 

When I first start eating, I'm usually still vibrating with whatever upset me—like that anger from the fight with my husband, or just the crushing stress from a huge campaign launch at work. So I'm feeling all of that very intensely. And then, as I'm eating, it's this weird mix of... desperation, I guess? Like I'm frantically trying to soothe myself or swallow down the feelings. I remember a couple of weeks ago, my sister had dropped off these leftover cupcakes from my niece’s birthday party, and I was standing at the counter eating one after another, and I was actually crying. Like, real, hot tears running right down my face while I was chewing. So I'm definitely feeling things. 

And then, as it goes on, the anger sort of shifts into this overwhelming panic and disgust. I'll be looking at the empty wrappers or the bottom of the Tupperware, and this wave of shame just hits me so hard it almost knocks the wind out of me. I'll think, "How did you let this happen again, Patricia? You're a grown woman, you manage a whole department of people, and you can't even stop yourself from eating a whole box of sweets." So, no, I wouldn't say I feel detached or numb at all. It’s just a really loud, messy storm of feelings, and the food is just... it's just me trying to drown it out, even though it never, ever works.
Do you usually have much less appetite in the morning, or do you often feel hungry when you wake up?

Appetite in the morning? Oh, gosh, no. No, I almost never have an appetite when I wake up. I mean, how could I, right? After eating all of that the night before, I usually wake up feeling so incredibly full, like physically heavy and bloated. It's this awful, sluggish feeling. I'll drag myself out of bed at, like, 6:00 AM because I have to get ready for work and check my emails before the daily briefing at 8:00, and the absolute last thing on my mind is food. 

Actually, just the thought of breakfast makes me feel a little nauseous. My husband—when we are speaking, that is—he’ll be in the kitchen making his protein shake or scrambling eggs, and the smell of the eggs cooking... ugh, it just turns my stomach. I can't even look at it. I usually just pour myself a huge cup of black coffee, maybe two, and that's all I can handle. I tell myself, "Well, you certainly don't need the calories after last night," which is true, but it's also just that my body physically rejects the idea of eating. I don't usually start feeling even a little bit hungry until maybe 1:00 or 2:00 in the afternoon, and even then, I try to hold off because I feel like I'm still paying penance for the binge, you know? But morning hunger? No, definitely not. It's just coffee and guilt for breakfast, pretty much every day.
During these nighttime eating episodes, do you feel like you're not in control of your eating—like you can't stop eating once you start, even if you wanted to?

Yes. Yes, exactly that. It’s... well, it ties right back into what I was trying to explain earlier about being aware but feeling like a passenger. Once I actually start eating, especially after a really tense night with my husband—which, let's be honest, has been happening a lot lately with the way we've been bickering—it is exactly like I lose all control. 

It's the most bizarre feeling because, you know, I make a hundred decisions a day. I run a whole marketing department, I have to be sharp, I direct people, I manage budgets. I am completely in control from 8 AM to 6 PM. But the second I open that fridge or pantry at night, it feels like the decision-making part of my brain just completely goes offline. It just unplugs. 

I'll be standing there, and my hand will just keep reaching for more food, over and over. I'll be grabbing another handful of pretzels or scooping out more of whatever is in the Tupperware, and the whole time my inner voice is right there, practically begging me. I'm literally thinking, "Patricia, stop, this is enough. You don't need this." I hear it so clearly! But there is this total, absolute disconnect between what my logical brain is pleading with me to do and what my hands are actually doing. I just can't make myself stop, even when I desperately want to. It’s like a runaway train, and I'm just watching myself do it, completely powerless to hit the brakes. It's so incredibly humiliating to be so capable in every other area of my life and then just completely lose all agency over a box of crackers, you know?

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with recurrent episodes of binge eating, a sense of lack of control during these episodes, marked distress, and associated daytime sequelae including guilt and lack of appetite in the morning. There is no evidence of compensatory behaviors such as purging, fasting, or excessive exercise, which rules out bulimia nervosa (F50.2). The clinical presentation aligns with binge-eating disorder (F50.8).
